From the City map of established neighbourhood energy systems (March 2020; boundaries illustrative only), placed to about ±150 m; consistent with the operator's description (between Boundary Road and Kerr Street). Hot water at 85 °C supply, 65 °C return; 15 MW; 20 buildings (CEEDC inventory, reported 2018). Buildings must be hydronic and designed for at most 70 °C supply and 50 °C return in peak winter, 45/40 °C in summer, with no gas, electric-resistance or conventional heat-pump heating (RDE Information for Developers, Sept 2018). Connection rules and rates not yet read (BCUC filings). Whether it takes heat from others is not published.

From the City map of established neighbourhood energy systems (March 2020; boundaries illustrative only), placed to about ±150 m. Steam, 237 MW, 220 buildings (CEEDC inventory, reported 2014); the 2012 Neighbourhood Energy Strategy gives more than 200 downtown buildings on steam and aims to convert it to low-carbon sources. Whether connection is required is not yet read. 2026 rates average $14.78 per thousand pounds of steam and $42.59/MWh on its hot-water networks (Northeast False Creek, Butterfly), the same price at the tariff's 0.347 MWh per thousand pounds (BCUC Order G-179-26, Aug 2026). The existing Beatty steam plant is past its design life and is being kept running until a New Beatty Energy Centre is built (maintenance planned to 2029). Rates follow a flat-rate and declining-block structure; a low-carbon service from the Core Steam Decarbonization Project (approved 2022, capital cost revised from $37.5 M to $52.6 M) was aimed for Q4 2025, but its first rate-design application was rejected as incomplete in September 2024 (BCUC Order G-252-24). Steam cannot take server heat without a large lift.
